title: Build your first project
description: Go from a name to a working Ansible project: two servers in two groups, shared settings, a playbook with a role, a site playbook, then check and export it.
outcomes: List servers in an inventory and sort them into groups
Share settings across a group with group vars
Write a play that targets a group and runs a role
Let Checks catch a missing role and scaffold it
Tie everything together with a site playbook, then review and export

checks.dbGroup: It sits in the db group
checks.playHosts: The play runs on the web group
checks.playRole: The play uses the nginx role
checks.scaffolded: The nginx role is in the project

recap: A project starts from a name. Everything else can change later.
The inventory says which servers exist; groups let one play reach many of them at once.
Group vars hold settings once for a whole group, in a file Ansible loads by name.
A play answers two questions: which hosts, and which roles to run on them.
Checks reads the whole project and offers fixes, like scaffolding a role nothing provides yet.
site.yml is the single entry point that runs your playbooks in order.
Architecture shows how it all connects; Export hands you files, a preset or a CLI command.

steps.intro: Let's build a small but real Ansible project: a web server and a database server. I'll drive and explain why each piece exists. Pause whenever you want, and you'll get your hands on it a few times.
steps.name: Every project starts with a name. kikx uses it for the output folder and as the default name for your files.
steps.start: That's all it needs. Start building opens the builder.
steps.path: An empty project shows the usual path: say which servers you have, configure them, then deploy. We'll follow it from the top.
steps.inventory: First, the inventory. Ansible can't do anything until it knows which machines exist and how to reach them.
steps.inventoryName: The inventory takes the project name. The file it writes is named after it, so you can keep one per environment.
steps.hostName: Each host gets a short name. It's how you'll refer to the server in playbooks and logs,
steps.hostAddress: and an address: the IP or DNS name Ansible opens an SSH connection to.
steps.hostGroup: Then a group. Groups are the real power of an inventory: a play targets a group, never a list of servers you'd have to keep in sync.
steps.previewGroup: The live preview shows the file exactly as it lands in your repo. Each [group] header lists the hosts that belong to it.
steps.addHost: Your turn. A database doesn't belong with the web servers, so add a second host in its own group: click Add host, name it db1, give it the address 10.0.0.20 and put it in a group called db.
steps.previewDb: Two groups now. Later you can run web tasks on web and database tasks on db, from the same file, without touching the other servers.
steps.addInventory: Add the inventory to the project. Nothing leaves your browser until you export.
steps.groupVars: Next, group vars: settings that every host in a group shares, like the port a web server listens on.
steps.groupName: Pick the group these settings apply to. Here, web.
steps.varKey: Then add a setting: a key and its value.
steps.varLine: This line goes into group_vars/web.yml. Ansible loads that file automatically for every host in web, just because of its name. db1 never sees it.
steps.varsWhy: Why not set it on each host? With ten web servers you'd repeat it ten times and forget one. A group var is written once, and a single host can still override it when it really differs.
steps.addVars: Add the group vars to the project.
steps.playbook: Now the part that does the work: a playbook. It describes what should happen on which servers.
steps.playbookName: Name it after what it configures. This one sets up the web tier.
steps.play: A playbook is a list of plays. Each play answers two questions: which hosts to run on, and which roles to run there.
steps.playName: Each play gets a name of its own. Ansible prints it as a heading while it runs, so you can follow along in the output.
steps.targetWeb: Your turn. Make this play run on the web group, then add a role called nginx and press Enter. The preview updates as you go.
steps.roleLine: A role is a reusable bundle of tasks, files and handlers. The play only names it; the role does the work, so the same role can serve many playbooks.
steps.addPlaybook: Add the playbook to the project.
steps.rolesMissing: Checks noticed something at once: this play uses nginx, but nothing in the project provides that role. Ansible would stop with a role not found error.
steps.checksTab: The Checks tab gathers every note across the project: errors first, then warnings and hints, each with a way to fix it or jump to the right component.
steps.checksNote: Here's the same note, with the same fix. Both buttons do exactly the same thing.
steps.backToBuild: Let's go back to the builder and fix it there.
steps.scaffold: Your turn. Click the scaffold button in the note above the form to create the missing role.
steps.scaffoldWhy: kikx added a role skeleton under roles/nginx: tasks, defaults, handlers and meta files. It's empty but valid, so the playbook runs today and you fill in real tasks when you're ready.
steps.site: Last file: a site playbook. It's the single entry point, ansible-playbook site.yml, that runs your playbooks in a fixed order.
steps.siteImport: kikx lists the playbooks this project produces. One click imports the web playbook.
steps.importLine: Each import_playbook line runs in turn, top to bottom. When you add a database playbook later, you add one line here and site.yml still runs everything.
steps.addSite: Add the site playbook to the project.
steps.diagram: Architecture draws what you built, so you can check it at a glance.
steps.diagramRead: Read it from left to right: your groups, with the group vars attached to web, then the playbooks, where site.yml imports web.yml, which targets web and runs its role. Anything left unconnected stands out here first.
steps.export: When you're happy, Export takes the project out of kikx.
steps.exportOptions: Files gives you a zip to drop into your repo. A preset saves the whole project so you can reopen it here or replay it with the CLI. CLI command copies the kikx command that writes the same files on your machine.
steps.done: That's a complete project: inventory, group vars, a playbook with its role, and a site playbook, all checked. Look around this demo project, or go back to yours.
